31  Spectral Graph Theory, Diffusion Maps, and Graph Laplacians

Graph algorithms translate into numerical linear algebra once edge weights and vertex degrees are assembled into matrices. Undirected graphs lead to symmetric positive semidefinite Laplacians whose spectra characterize connectivity and graph cuts. Random walks and diffusion maps generalize these spectra to nonlinear manifold learning, offering multiscale geometric filtering and permutation-invariant representations for physical systems.

31.1 Graph Matrices and the Laplacian

NoteDefinition: Adjacency and Degree Matrices

For a weighted undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(n\) vertices:

  • Adjacency \(\bA\): \(A_{ij} = w_{ij} \geq 0\) if \((i,j) \in E\), and \(A_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. We assume \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\) and \(A_{ii} = 0\).

  • Degree \(\bD\): Diagonal matrix with entries \(D_{ii} = d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}\).

NoteDefinition: Unnormalized Graph Laplacian

The unnormalized graph Laplacian is \[ \begin{align} \bL = \bD - \bA. \end{align} \] For any signal \(\bx \in \fR^n\) on the vertices, the action of \(\bL\) acts as a discrete Laplace operator: \[ \begin{align} (\bL \bx)_i = \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j). \end{align} \] The associated quadratic form satisfies \[ \begin{align} \bx^T \bL \bx = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2. \end{align} \]

NoteProposition: Laplacian Positive Semidefinite

For an undirected graph with nonnegative weights, \(\bL\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and \(\bL\mathbf{1}=\bzero\).

TipProof

Symmetry follows from \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\), so \(\bA = \bA^T\) and \(\bL = \bD - \bA = \bL^T\). Expanding the quadratic form algebraically from definitions: \[ \begin{align} \bx^T \bL \bx &= \bx^T (\bD - \bA) \bx = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} \right) x_i^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_j^2 - \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} x_i x_j \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2 = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2. \end{align} \] Because \(w_{ij} \geq 0\) and \((x_i - x_j)^2 \geq 0\), each term is non-negative, so \(\bx^T \bL \bx \geq 0\) for all \(\bx \in \fR^n\), proving positive semidefiniteness. For \(\bx = \mathbf{1}\), every coordinate satisfies \((\bL\mathbf{1})_i = d_i - \sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij} = 0\), so \(\bL\mathbf{1} = \bzero\).

NoteTheorem: Spectral Properties of the Graph Laplacian

Let the eigenvalues of \(\bL\) be ordered as \(0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq ... \leq \lambda_n\).

  1. \(\lambda_1 = 0\) with eigenvector \(\bv_1 = \mathbf{1}\).

  2. The multiplicity of eigenvalue \(0\) equals the number of connected components of \(G\).

  3. The second smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) is the algebraic connectivity (Fiedler value). It satisfies \(\lambda_2 > 0\) if and only if \(G\) is connected.

TipProof

Proposition~above shows that all eigenvalues of \(\bL\) are nonnegative and that \(\mathbf{1}\in\ker(\bL)\), so \(\lambda_1=0\).

It remains to identify the entire nullspace. If \(\bx\in\ker(\bL)\), then \[ \begin{align} 0=\bx^T\bL\bx=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2. \end{align} \] Every term is nonnegative. Hence \(x_i=x_j\) across every edge with positive weight, and therefore \(\bx\) is constant on each connected component. Conversely, a vector that is constant on each connected component has zero difference across every edge and belongs to \(\ker(\bL)\). The indicator vectors of the connected components form a basis for this nullspace, so the multiplicity of eigenvalue zero equals the number of components.

In particular, \(G\) is connected exactly when \(\ker(\bL)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}\). In that case zero is a simple eigenvalue, so \(\lambda_2>0\). If \(G\) is disconnected, the nullspace has dimension at least two and \(\lambda_2=0\).

NoteCorollary: Rayleigh Characterization of Algebraic Connectivity

For a connected undirected graph, \[ \begin{align} \lambda_2 =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero} \frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx} =\min_{\bx\perp\mathbf{1},\,\bx\neq\bzero} \frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2}{\sum_i x_i^2}. \end{align} \]

TipProof

By the result above, a connected graph has an orthonormal eigenbasis with \(\bq_1=\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{n}\) and \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\). If \(\bx\perp\mathbf{1}\), then \(\bx=\sum_{k=2}^n c_k\bq_k\), and \[ \begin{align} \frac{\bx^T\bL\bx}{\bx^T\bx} =\frac{\sum_{k=2}^n\lambda_k c_k^2}{\sum_{k=2}^n c_k^2} \geq\lambda_2. \end{align} \] Equality holds for a Fiedler eigenvector \(\bq_2\). The second expression follows from the result above.

NoteDefinition: Normalized Laplacians

Normalized Laplacians account for high-degree vertices:

  • Symmetric Normalized Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{sym}} = \bD^{-1/2} \bL \bD^{-1/2} = \bI - \bD^{-1/2} \bA \bD^{-1/2}\). Its spectrum lies in the interval \([0, 2]\).

  • Random Walk Laplacian: \(\bL_{\text{rw}} = \bD^{-1} \bL = \bI - \bD^{-1} \bA\). It is similar to \(\bL_{\text{sym}}\) and shares its eigenvalues.

31.2 Spectral Clustering

NoteTheorem: Spectral Relaxation of Graph Cuts

Partitioning a graph into two disjoint sets \(A\) and \(B\) to minimize the normalized cut is NP-hard. Relaxing the discrete indicator vector to a continuous vector subject to an orthogonality constraint yields the Rayleigh quotient problem \[ \begin{align} \min_{\bx \perp \bD\mathbf{1},\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bL \bx}{\bx^T \bD \bx}. \end{align} \] The optimal solution is the Fiedler eigenvector \(\bv_2\) of the generalized eigenvalue problem \(\bL \bv = \lambda \bD \bv\), or equivalently the second eigenvector of \(\bL_{\text{rw}}\). Spectral clustering embeds vertices in \(\fR^k\) using the first \(k\) nontrivial eigenvectors, then partitions the coordinates using \(k\)-means.

31.3 Diffusion Maps and Nonlinear Manifolds

TipRemark

(From graphs to manifolds) When data points \(\bx_1, ..., \bx_N \in \fR^d\) lie on a low-dimensional manifold embedded in high-dimensional space, ambient Euclidean distances can obscure intrinsic connectivity or create shortcuts across a curved manifold. Diffusion maps define a random walk on a graph constructed over the point cloud and, under suitable sampling and bandwidth limits, approximate diffusion generated by a Laplace–Beltrami operator.

NoteDefinition: Diffusion Operator and Random Walk

Given point cloud \(\{\bx_i\}_{i=1}^N \subset \fR^d\), construct a pairwise affinity matrix \(\bK \in \fR^{N \times N}\) using a Gaussian kernel with bandwidth \(\delta > 0\): \[ \begin{align} K_{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2}{2\delta^2}\right). \end{align} \] Let \(d_i = \sum_{j=1}^N K_{ij}\) denote the row sums, and define \(\bD = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, ..., d_N)\). The row-stochastic diffusion matrix is \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{M} = \bD^{-1} \bK. \end{align} \] The entry \(M_{ij} = K_{ij}/d_i\) defines the transition probability from point \(\bx_i\) to point \(\bx_j\) in a single diffusion step.

NoteTheorem: Spectral Decomposition of the Diffusion Operator

The matrix \(\mathbf{M} = \bD^{-1}\bK\) is similar to the real symmetric matrix \[ \begin{align} \bS = \bD^{-1/2} \bK \bD^{-1/2} = \bD^{1/2} \mathbf{M} \bD^{-1/2}. \end{align} \] Let \(\bS = \bV \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bV^T\) be the eigendecomposition of \(\bS\) with orthonormal eigenvectors \(\bV = [\bv_0, \bv_1, ..., \bv_{N-1}]\) and eigenvalues \[ \begin{align} 1 = \lambda_0 > \lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq ... \geq \lambda_{N-1} \geq 0. \end{align} \] Then \(\mathbf{M}\) has real eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) with right eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{\psi}_k = \bD^{-1/2}\bv_k\) and left eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_k = \bD^{1/2}\bv_k\). The right eigenvectors satisfy \(\mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\psi}_k = \lambda_k \boldsymbol{\psi}_k\), with \(\boldsymbol{\psi}_0 = \mathbf{1}\).

TipProof

Because \(\bK\) is symmetric and strictly positive, \(\bS = \bD^{-1/2}\bK\bD^{-1/2}\) is real symmetric. By the spectral theorem (the result above), \(\bS = \bV\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bV^T\) with orthonormal eigenvectors \(\bV^T\bV = \bI\). Rewriting the similarity relation: \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{M} = \bD^{-1/2} \bS \bD^{1/2}. \end{align} \] Multiplying by \(\boldsymbol{\psi}_k = \bD^{-1/2}\bv_k\): \[ \begin{align} \mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\psi}_k = \left( \bD^{-1/2}\bS\bD^{1/2} \right) \left( \bD^{-1/2}\bv_k \right) = \bD^{-1/2}\bS\bv_k = \lambda_k \bD^{-1/2}\bv_k = \lambda_k \boldsymbol{\psi}_k. \end{align} \] Similarly, defining left eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{\phi}_k = \bD^{1/2}\bv_k\): \[ \begin{align} \boldsymbol{\phi}_k^T\mathbf{M} = \left(\bD^{1/2}\bv_k\right)^T \left(\bD^{-1/2}\bS\bD^{1/2}\right) = \bv_k^T\bS\bD^{1/2} = \lambda_k \bv_k^T\bD^{1/2} = \lambda_k \boldsymbol{\phi}_k^T. \end{align} \] Biorthogonality follows directly: \[ \begin{align} \boldsymbol{\phi}_j^T \boldsymbol{\psi}_k = \left(\bD^{1/2}\bv_j\right)^T \left(\bD^{-1/2}\bv_k\right) = \bv_j^T\bv_k = \delta_{jk}. \end{align} \] Because \(\mathbf{M}\) is row-stochastic, \(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\), so \(\lambda_0 = 1\) with right eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{\psi}_0 = \mathbf{1}\).

NoteDefinition: Diffusion Distance and Diffusion Map Coordinates

The \(t\)-step diffusion operator \(\mathbf{M}^t\) represents running the random walk forward for time \(t\). The diffusion distance between points \(\bx_i\) and \(\bx_j\) measures the difference between their conditional transition distributions weighted by the stationary measure \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\): \[ \begin{align} D_t(\bx_i, \bx_j)^2 = \|\mathbf{M}^t(i, :) - \mathbf{M}^t(j, :)\|_{\bD^{-1}}^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} \lambda_k^{2t} \big(\psi_k(i) - \psi_k(j)\big)^2. \end{align} \] The diffusion map embedding of point \(\bx_i\) into an \(m\)-dimensional Euclidean space is \[ \begin{align} \Psi_t(\bx_i) = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^t \psi_1(i) \\ \lambda_2^t \psi_2(i) \\ \vdots \\ \lambda_m^t \psi_m(i) \end{pmatrix} \in \fR^m. \end{align} \] Under this embedding, Euclidean distance in \(\fR^m\) equals the truncated diffusion distance: \[ \begin{align} \|\Psi_t(\bx_i) - \Psi_t(\bx_j)\|_2^2 \approx D_t(\bx_i, \bx_j)^2. \end{align} \]

TipRemark

(Diffusion time as a geometric low-pass filter) The factor \(\lambda_k^{2t}\) in the diffusion distance acts as an exponential low-pass filter on manifold coordinates. Because \(\lambda_k < 1\) for all \(k \geq 1\), increasing \(t\) rapidly suppresses high-frequency modes associated with small eigenvalues, leaving only the dominant macroscopic geometric coordinates.

31.4 Permutation Invariance and Graph Spectra

TipRemark

(Combinatorial bottleneck in coordinate representations) In molecular systems and particle clusters with \(N\) identical atoms, the state is specified by atomic positions in \(\fR^{3N}\). Comparing two configurations \(\bx, \by \in \fR^{3N}\) directly requires optimizing over all \(N!\) atomic index permutations \(\sigma \in S_N\), in addition to Euclidean rotations and translations. This combinatorial alignment cost is intractable for moderate \(N\).

NoteTheorem: Permutation Invariance of Graph Spectra

Let \(\bD \in \fR^{N \times N}\) be the pairwise interatomic distance matrix with entries \(D_{ij} = \|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\). Under any atom permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), the distance matrix transforms by an orthogonal permutation matrix \(\bP_\sigma\): \[ \begin{align} \bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T. \end{align} \] Let \(\bL\) be any graph Laplacian constructed from edge weights \(w_{ij} = f(D_{ij})\). Then the permuted Laplacian is \[ \begin{align} \bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T. \end{align} \] Because \(\bP_\sigma\) is orthogonal, \(\bL_\sigma\) is orthogonally similar to \(\bL\). Therefore, the eigenvalue spectrum \[ \begin{align} \operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, ..., \lambda_N) \end{align} \] is invariant under all atomic permutations \(\sigma \in S_N\) and all rigid Euclidean isometries \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).

TipProof

Because rigid rotations and translations preserve pairwise distances \(\|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\|_2\), the matrix \(\bD\) is invariant under \(\mathrm{SE}(3)\).

Under a permutation \(\sigma \in S_N\), vertex \(i\) maps to \(\sigma(i)\), so the permuted affinity matrix has entries \(W_{\sigma(i), \sigma(j)} = W_{ij}\). In matrix notation, \(\bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bW \bP_\sigma^T\). Similarly, the degree matrix transforms as \(\bD_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bD \bP_\sigma^T\). Thus \[ \begin{align} \bL_\sigma = \bD_\sigma - \bW_\sigma = \bP_\sigma (\bD - \bW) \bP_\sigma^T = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T. \end{align} \] Because permutation matrices are orthogonal (\(\bP_\sigma^{-1} = \bP_\sigma^T\)), the characteristic polynomial satisfies \[ \begin{align} \det(\bL_\sigma - \lambda \bI) = \det(\bP_\sigma (\bL - \lambda \bI) \bP_\sigma^T) = \det(\bP_\sigma)\det(\bL - \lambda \bI)\det(\bP_\sigma^T) = \det(\bL - \lambda \bI). \end{align} \] The roots of the characteristic polynomial are identical. Thus the eigenvalue multiset \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL)\) is invariant under any relabeling of identical particles.

31.5 Bandwidth Selection via Affinity Scaling

TipRemark

(Sigmoidal behavior of the affinity sum) The Gaussian affinity kernel \(K_{ij} = \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\) requires selecting the bandwidth parameter \(\delta\). If \(\delta\) is too small, points are isolated and \(K_{ij} \approx 0\) for \(i \neq j\). If \(\delta\) is too large, points are fully connected and \(K_{ij} \approx 1\).

Define the total affinity sum \[ \begin{align} S(\delta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \exp\left(-\frac{\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2}{2\delta^2}\right). \end{align} \] Plotting \(\ln S(\delta)\) against \(\ln \delta\) yields a sigmoidal curve:

  1. As \(\delta \to 0\), \(K_{ij} \to 0\) for \(i \neq j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to \ln N\).

  2. As \(\delta \to \infty\), \(K_{ij} \to 1\) for all \(i,j\), so \(S(\delta) \to N^2\) and \(\ln S(\delta) \to 2\ln N\).

  3. In the intermediate scaling regime, \(S(\delta) \propto \delta^d\), where \(d\) is the intrinsic manifold dimension. The slope \(\frac{d\ln S(\delta)}{d\ln \delta} \approx d\) estimates dimension.

Choosing \(\delta\) in the linear transition regime ensures that the kernel resolves intrinsic manifold geometry without collapsing into disconnected points or a uniform complete graph.

31.6 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Compute. (Path graph Laplacian spectrum) For a three-node unweighted path graph \(1-2-3\), write down \(\bA\) and \(\bL\). Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\bL\) by hand. Verify that \(\lambda_1 = 0\) with \(\bv_1 = (1, 1, 1)^T\), and compute the algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2\).

  2. Derive. (Rayleigh quotient for algebraic connectivity) For the path graph in the preceding exercise, minimize the quotient in the result above over vectors of the form \((a,b,-a-b)^T\). Verify that the minimum equals the computed value of \(\lambda_2\). Then evaluate the numerator on a two-level vector that is constant on each side of a proposed cut and explain how weak cross-cut weights lower its energy.

  3. Derive. (Permutation invariance of graph spectra) Consider a cluster of four identical atoms in \(\fR^3\).

    1. Let the coordinates be arranged in a vector \(\bx \in \fR^{12}\). Explain why comparing two configurations \(\bx\) and \(\by\) requires testing \(4! = 24\) permutations.

    2. Construct the interatomic distance matrix \(\bD\) and form the graph Laplacian \(\bL\). Prove that for any permutation \(\sigma \in S_4\), \(\bL_\sigma = \bP_\sigma \bL \bP_\sigma^T\).

    3. Explain how sorting the eigenvalues \(\operatorname{spec}(\bL) = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_4)\) produces a coordinate-free, permutation-invariant fingerprint for molecular structure.

  4. Explore. (Diffusion time as a geometric low-pass filter) Let a diffusion operator on a data manifold have leading eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 0.98\) and \(\lambda_2 = 0.80\).

    1. Compute the ratio of modal contributions \((\lambda_2 / \lambda_1)^{2t}\) for diffusion times \(t = 1\), \(t = 5\), and \(t = 20\).

    2. Explain why increasing \(t\) contracts local high-frequency fluctuations while preserving macroscopic manifold geometry.

    3. What happens to the diffusion distance \(D_t(\bx_i, \bx_j)\) as \(t \to \infty\)?

  5. Explore. (Sigmoidal bandwidth selection) Let \(N = 100\) data points be sampled uniformly from a circle of radius \(R = 1\) in \(\fR^2\).

    1. Write down the formula for the affinity sum \(S(\delta) = \sum_{i,j} \exp(-\|\bx_i - \bx_j\|^2 / (2\delta^2))\).

    2. Evaluate the asymptotic limits of \(\ln S(\delta)\) as \(\delta \to 0\) and \(\delta \to \infty\).

    3. In the intermediate scaling regime \(\delta \in [0.1, 0.5]\), show that the slope \(\frac{d\ln S(\delta)}{d\ln \delta} \approx 1\), reflecting the one-dimensional geometry of the circle.

ImportantLiterature trail: Diffusion distance from the source

Read Ronald R.~Coifman and St'ephane Lafon’s 2006 paper, Diffusion Maps (Coifman and Lafon 2006).

Search hint. The title, authors, and year identify the article in Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis.

Mathematical hint. The normalization is not cosmetic. Follow the measure with respect to which the Markov operator is reversible, and only then expand the diffusion distance spectrally.

  1. Give a complete citation and locate the definition of diffusion distance.

  2. Translate the kernel, normalization, Markov operator, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors into this chapter’s notation.

  3. State the assumptions under which the spectral representation is valid, including the role of the stationary measure.

  4. Reconstruct the spectral identity for diffusion distance. Then explain what the paper’s anisotropic normalization changes and why that issue is invisible if one treats a graph Laplacian as an arbitrary symmetric matrix.

NoteFurther reading

Chung develops spectral graph theory from the graph-Laplacian side (Chung 1997). Belkin and Niyogi introduce Laplacian eigenmaps, while Coifman and Lafon develop diffusion maps and the normalization used in the literature trail (Belkin and Niyogi 2003; Coifman and Lafon 2006).

Belkin, Mikhail, and Partha Niyogi. 2003. “Laplacian Eigenmaps for Dimensionality Reduction and Data Representation.” Neural Computation 15 (6): 1373–96. https://doi.org/10.1162/089976603321780317.
Chung, Fan R. K. 1997. Spectral Graph Theory. Vol. 92. CBMS Regional Conference Series in Mathematics. American Mathematical Society.
Coifman, Ronald R., and Stéphane Lafon. 2006. “Diffusion Maps.” Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis 21 (1): 5–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.acha.2006.04.006.
